# Left and Right Inverses of a Square Matrix over a Field are Equal

## 0. Statement, and a remark on its wording

Let $\Bbb F$ be a field (for instance one of $\Q$, $\R$, $\C$; no special property of these is
used below). Let $n \in \Z_{>0}$, and let $\mathcal M \left({n}\right)$ denote the matrix space of
order $n$ square matrices over $\Bbb F$. Let $\mathbf A, \mathbf B \in \mathcal M \left({n}\right)$.

Recall the definitions, where $\mathbf I_n$ denotes the $n \times n$ identity matrix:

* $\mathbf B$ is a **left inverse** of $\mathbf A$ if and only if $\mathbf{BA} = \mathbf I_n$;
* $\mathbf B$ is a **right inverse** of $\mathbf A$ if and only if $\mathbf{AB} = \mathbf I_n$.

> **Theorem.**
> 1. If $\mathbf B$ is a left inverse of $\mathbf A$, then $\mathbf B$ is also a right inverse of $\mathbf A$.
> 2. If $\mathbf B$ is a right inverse of $\mathbf A$, then $\mathbf B$ is also a left inverse of $\mathbf A$.
>
> Consequently, in either case $\mathbf{AB} = \mathbf{BA} = \mathbf I_n$, so that $\mathbf B$ is a
> two-sided inverse of $\mathbf A$; and any left inverse of $\mathbf A$ is equal to any right
> inverse of $\mathbf A$.

**Remark on the wording of the problem.** The final clause of the problem as posed reads: "let
$\mathbf B$ be a right inverse matrix of $\mathbf A$; then $\mathbf B$ is also a *right* inverse
matrix of $\mathbf A$". Read literally this is the tautology $P \implies P$ (true, but vacuous);
it is evidently a typographical slip for "then $\mathbf B$ is also a *left* inverse matrix of
$\mathbf A$", which is the assertion dual to the first half and the one matching the title of the
problem. We prove that intended statement; it is Part 2 above. So the claim of the problem, on its
intended reading, is **true**, and nothing needs correcting beyond this slip of wording.

Note also that, since we prove both implications, the theorem is insensitive to which of the two
possible naming conventions for "left inverse" is adopted: under the opposite convention
(*$\mathbf B$ is a left inverse of $\mathbf A$ iff $\mathbf{AB} = \mathbf I_n$*) Parts 1 and 2
simply exchange places.

The proof of Part 1 is given in Section 3; Part 2 is deduced from Part 1 by a symmetry argument.
Section 4 gives an independent proof by determinants, and Section 5 shows that the hypotheses are
sharp.

## 1. Conventions and elementary facts about matrices

For $m, p \in \Z_{>0}$ let $\mathcal M \left({m, p}\right)$ denote the set of $m \times p$ matrices
over $\Bbb F$, and write $\left[{\mathbf M}\right]_{i j}$ for the entry of $\mathbf M$ in row $i$
and column $j$. Matrix multiplication is defined as usual: for
$\mathbf M \in \mathcal M \left({m, p}\right)$ and $\mathbf N \in \mathcal M \left({p, q}\right)$,
the product $\mathbf{MN} \in \mathcal M \left({m, q}\right)$ has entries
$$\left[{\mathbf{MN}}\right]_{i j} = \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^p \left[{\mathbf M}\right]_{i k} \left[{\mathbf N}\right]_{k j} .$$
Note that $\mathcal M \left({n}\right) = \mathcal M \left({n, n}\right)$. We shall use the following
elementary facts.

**(M1) Associativity.** For $\mathbf M \in \mathcal M \left({m, p}\right)$,
$\mathbf N \in \mathcal M \left({p, q}\right)$, $\mathbf P \in \mathcal M \left({q, r}\right)$:
$\left({\mathbf{MN}}\right) \mathbf P = \mathbf M \left({\mathbf{NP}}\right)$.

*Proof.* For all $i, l$:
$$\left[{\left({\mathbf{MN}}\right) \mathbf P}\right]_{i l}
= \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^q \left({\sum_{k \mathop = 1}^p \left[{\mathbf M}\right]_{i k} \left[{\mathbf N}\right]_{k j}}\right) \left[{\mathbf P}\right]_{j l}
= \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^q \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^p \left[{\mathbf M}\right]_{i k} \left[{\mathbf N}\right]_{k j} \left[{\mathbf P}\right]_{j l} ,$$
$$\left[{\mathbf M \left({\mathbf{NP}}\right)}\right]_{i l}
= \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^p \left[{\mathbf M}\right]_{i k} \left({\sum_{j \mathop = 1}^q \left[{\mathbf N}\right]_{k j} \left[{\mathbf P}\right]_{j l}}\right)
= \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^p \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^q \left[{\mathbf M}\right]_{i k} \left[{\mathbf N}\right]_{k j} \left[{\mathbf P}\right]_{j l} ,$$
using distributivity and associativity of multiplication in $\Bbb F$. The two iterated finite sums
have the same terms and are equal, by commutativity and associativity of addition in $\Bbb F$. $\Box$

**(M2) Identity.** With $\left[{\mathbf I_n}\right]_{i j} = \delta_{i j}$ (Kronecker delta), we have
$\mathbf I_m \mathbf M = \mathbf M = \mathbf M \mathbf I_p$ for
$\mathbf M \in \mathcal M \left({m, p}\right)$: indeed
$\left[{\mathbf I_m \mathbf M}\right]_{i j} = \sum_k \delta_{i k} \left[{\mathbf M}\right]_{k j}
= \left[{\mathbf M}\right]_{i j}$, and symmetrically on the other side.

We write $\Bbb F^n := \mathcal M \left({n, 1}\right)$ for the set of **column vectors** of length
$n$; with entrywise addition and scalar multiplication it is a vector space over $\Bbb F$. Let
$\mathbf e_1, \ldots, \mathbf e_n \in \Bbb F^n$ be the standard column vectors, defined by
$\left[{\mathbf e_j}\right]_{i 1} = \delta_{i j}$.

**(M3) Columns.** For $\mathbf M \in \mathcal M \left({n}\right)$ and $1 \le j \le n$, the vector
$\mathbf M \mathbf e_j \in \Bbb F^n$ is the $j$-th column of $\mathbf M$:
$$\left[{\mathbf M \mathbf e_j}\right]_{i 1} = \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n \left[{\mathbf M}\right]_{i k} \delta_{k j} = \left[{\mathbf M}\right]_{i j} .$$

**(M4) A matrix is determined by its action on $\mathbf e_1, \ldots, \mathbf e_n$.** If
$\mathbf M, \mathbf N \in \mathcal M \left({n}\right)$ satisfy $\mathbf M \mathbf e_j = \mathbf N \mathbf e_j$
for all $j \in \left\{{1, \ldots, n}\right\}$, then $\mathbf M = \mathbf N$.

*Proof.* By (M3), for all $i, j$ we get
$\left[{\mathbf M}\right]_{i j} = \left[{\mathbf M \mathbf e_j}\right]_{i 1} = \left[{\mathbf N \mathbf e_j}\right]_{i 1} = \left[{\mathbf N}\right]_{i j}$. $\Box$

For $\mathbf M \in \mathcal M \left({n}\right)$ define the map
$$T_{\mathbf M} : \Bbb F^n \to \Bbb F^n , \qquad T_{\mathbf M} \left({\mathbf x}\right) := \mathbf M \mathbf x .$$
(This is well defined: $\mathbf M \mathbf x \in \mathcal M \left({n, 1}\right) = \Bbb F^n$.)

**(M5)** $T_{\mathbf M}$ is linear; $T_{\mathbf{MN}} = T_{\mathbf M} \circ T_{\mathbf N}$ for
$\mathbf M, \mathbf N \in \mathcal M \left({n}\right)$; and $T_{\mathbf I_n} = \operatorname{id}_{\Bbb F^n}$.

*Proof.* Linearity: for $\mathbf x, \mathbf y \in \Bbb F^n$ and $\lambda, \mu \in \Bbb F$,
$$\left[{\mathbf M \left({\lambda \mathbf x + \mu \mathbf y}\right)}\right]_{i 1}
= \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n \left[{\mathbf M}\right]_{i k} \left({\lambda \left[{\mathbf x}\right]_{k 1} + \mu \left[{\mathbf y}\right]_{k 1}}\right)
= \lambda \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n \left[{\mathbf M}\right]_{i k} \left[{\mathbf x}\right]_{k 1}
 + \mu \sum_{k \mathop = 1}^n \left[{\mathbf M}\right]_{i k} \left[{\mathbf y}\right]_{k 1} ,$$
which is the $i$-th entry of $\lambda \left({\mathbf M \mathbf x}\right) + \mu \left({\mathbf M \mathbf y}\right)$;
here we used distributivity, commutativity and associativity in $\Bbb F$. Composition: for
$\mathbf x \in \Bbb F^n$, viewing $\mathbf x$ as an $n \times 1$ matrix, (M1) gives
$$T_{\mathbf{MN}} \left({\mathbf x}\right) = \left({\mathbf{MN}}\right) \mathbf x = \mathbf M \left({\mathbf N \mathbf x}\right)
= T_{\mathbf M} \left({T_{\mathbf N} \left({\mathbf x}\right)}\right) .$$
Finally $T_{\mathbf I_n} \left({\mathbf x}\right) = \mathbf I_n \mathbf x = \mathbf x$ by (M2). $\Box$

## 2. The linear algebra input

Let $V$ be a vector space over $\Bbb F$. A finite **list** (i.e. finite family, repetitions allowed)
$\mathbf v_1, \ldots, \mathbf v_k$ of vectors of $V$ is **linearly dependent** if and only if there
exist $c_1, \ldots, c_k \in \Bbb F$, **not all zero**, with
$\sum_{j \mathop = 1}^k c_j \mathbf v_j = \mathbf 0$; otherwise the list is **linearly independent**.
The **span** of the list is
$\left\{{\sum_{j \mathop = 1}^k c_j \mathbf v_j : c_1, \ldots, c_k \in \Bbb F}\right\}$, a subspace
of $V$; the span of the empty list ($k = 0$) is $\left\{{\mathbf 0}\right\}$. The list *spans* $V$
if its span is $V$.

**Lemma 1 (Steinitz exchange lemma, dependence form).** Let $V$ be a vector space over $\Bbb F$
spanned by a list $\mathbf u_1, \ldots, \mathbf u_m$ with $m \ge 0$. Then every list
$\mathbf w_1, \ldots, \mathbf w_k$ of vectors of $V$ with $k > m$ is linearly dependent.

*Proof.* By induction on $m \ge 0$; the statement to be proved for a given $m$ is quantified over
all $V$, all spanning lists of length $m$, all $k > m$ and all lists of length $k$.

*Base case $m = 0$.* Here $V = \left\{{\mathbf 0}\right\}$ and $k \ge 1$. Then
$\mathbf w_1 = \mathbf 0$, so
$1 \cdot \mathbf w_1 + 0 \cdot \mathbf w_2 + \cdots + 0 \cdot \mathbf w_k = \mathbf 0$ is a
dependence relation with a non-zero coefficient (in a field $1 \ne 0$). Hence the list is linearly
dependent.

*Induction step.* Let $m \ge 1$ and suppose the statement holds for $m - 1$. Let $V$ be spanned by
$\mathbf u_1, \ldots, \mathbf u_m$, let $k > m$, and let $\mathbf w_1, \ldots, \mathbf w_k \in V$.
Since the $\mathbf u_i$ span $V$, we may **choose** for each $j$ scalars $a_{1 j}, \ldots, a_{m j}$ with
$$\mathbf w_j = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^m a_{i j} \mathbf u_i . \tag{$*$}$$
(No uniqueness of these scalars is claimed or needed; we work with the chosen expressions.) Let $W$
denote the span of $\mathbf u_1, \ldots, \mathbf u_{m - 1}$, a subspace of $V$, hence itself a
vector space over $\Bbb F$ spanned by a list of length $m - 1$.

*Case 1: $a_{m j} = 0$ for every $j \in \left\{{1, \ldots, k}\right\}$.* Then by $(*)$ each
$\mathbf w_j \in W$. As $k > m > m - 1$, the induction hypothesis applied to $W$ and the list
$\mathbf w_1, \ldots, \mathbf w_k$ shows this list is linearly dependent, as required.

*Case 2: $a_{m l} \ne 0$ for some $l \in \left\{{1, \ldots, k}\right\}$.* Since $\Bbb F$ is a field,
$a_{m l}^{-1}$ exists. For each $j \ne l$ set
$$\mathbf w'_j := \mathbf w_j - a_{m j} a_{m l}^{-1} \mathbf w_l .$$
Substituting the expressions $(*)$ for $\mathbf w_j$ and $\mathbf w_l$ and collecting terms,
$$\mathbf w'_j = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^m \left({a_{i j} - a_{m j} a_{m l}^{-1} a_{i l}}\right) \mathbf u_i ,$$
and the coefficient of $\mathbf u_m$ in this particular expression is
$a_{m j} - a_{m j} a_{m l}^{-1} a_{m l} = a_{m j} - a_{m j} = 0$. Hence
$$\mathbf w'_j = \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^{m - 1} \left({a_{i j} - a_{m j} a_{m l}^{-1} a_{i l}}\right) \mathbf u_i \in W \qquad \text{for all } j \ne l .$$
The list $\left({\mathbf w'_j}\right)_{j \ne l}$ consists of $k - 1$ vectors of $W$ (re-index
the set $\left\{{1, \ldots, k}\right\} \setminus \left\{{l}\right\}$ as $1, \ldots, k - 1$ if a
list indexed by an initial segment is wanted; this affects nothing), and $k - 1 > m - 1$ because
$k > m$. By the induction hypothesis it is linearly dependent: there are scalars
$\left({c_j}\right)_{j \ne l}$, not all zero, with $\sum_{j \ne l} c_j \mathbf w'_j = \mathbf 0$.
Expanding the definition of $\mathbf w'_j$,
$$\mathbf 0 = \sum_{j \ne l} c_j \left({\mathbf w_j - a_{m j} a_{m l}^{-1} \mathbf w_l}\right)
= \sum_{j \ne l} c_j \mathbf w_j + \left({- \sum_{j \ne l} c_j a_{m j} a_{m l}^{-1}}\right) \mathbf w_l .$$
This is a linear dependence relation among $\mathbf w_1, \ldots, \mathbf w_k$ (the coefficient of
$\mathbf w_j$ being $c_j$ for $j \ne l$, and $- \sum_{j \ne l} c_j a_{m j} a_{m l}^{-1}$ for
$j = l$), and it is non-trivial, since by hypothesis $c_j \ne 0$ for at least one $j \ne l$.
Hence $\mathbf w_1, \ldots, \mathbf w_k$ is linearly dependent.

In both cases the conclusion holds, completing the induction. $\Box$

**Lemma 2.** The list $\mathbf e_1, \ldots, \mathbf e_n$ spans $\Bbb F^n$ and is linearly
independent. Consequently every list of $n + 1$ vectors of $\Bbb F^n$ is linearly dependent.

*Proof.* *Spanning:* for $\mathbf x \in \Bbb F^n$ put $c_j := \left[{\mathbf x}\right]_{j 1}$; then
for each $i$,
$\left[{\sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n c_j \mathbf e_j}\right]_{i 1} = \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n c_j \delta_{i j} = c_i = \left[{\mathbf x}\right]_{i 1}$,
so $\mathbf x = \sum_j c_j \mathbf e_j$. *Independence:* if $\sum_j c_j \mathbf e_j = \mathbf 0$
then, taking the $i$-th entry as just computed, $c_i = 0$, for each $i$. The last sentence is
Lemma 1 applied with the spanning list $\mathbf e_1, \ldots, \mathbf e_n$ (so $m = n$) and
$k = n + 1 > n$. $\Box$

**Lemma 3.** Any linearly independent list $\mathbf v_1, \ldots, \mathbf v_n$ of $n$ vectors of
$\Bbb F^n$ spans $\Bbb F^n$.

*Proof.* Let $\mathbf w \in \Bbb F^n$ be arbitrary. The list
$\mathbf v_1, \ldots, \mathbf v_n, \mathbf w$ has $n + 1$ members, so by Lemma 2 it is linearly
dependent: there are $c_1, \ldots, c_n, c \in \Bbb F$, not all zero, with
$$\sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n c_j \mathbf v_j + c \mathbf w = \mathbf 0 .$$
If $c = 0$, this reads $\sum_j c_j \mathbf v_j = \mathbf 0$ with $c_1, \ldots, c_n$ not all zero
(as not all of $c_1, \ldots, c_n, c$ are zero and $c = 0$), contradicting the linear independence
of $\mathbf v_1, \ldots, \mathbf v_n$. Hence $c \ne 0$; as $\Bbb F$ is a field, $c^{-1}$ exists and
$$\mathbf w = \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n \left({- c^{-1} c_j}\right) \mathbf v_j ,$$
so $\mathbf w$ lies in the span of $\mathbf v_1, \ldots, \mathbf v_n$. As $\mathbf w$ was
arbitrary, that span is all of $\Bbb F^n$. $\Box$

**Lemma 4 (an injective linear endomorphism of $\Bbb F^n$ is surjective).** Let
$T : \Bbb F^n \to \Bbb F^n$ be linear and injective. Then $T$ is surjective, and hence bijective.

*Proof.* First, the list $T \left({\mathbf e_1}\right), \ldots, T \left({\mathbf e_n}\right)$ is
linearly independent. Indeed, suppose $\sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n c_j T \left({\mathbf e_j}\right) = \mathbf 0$.
By linearity $T \left({\sum_j c_j \mathbf e_j}\right) = \mathbf 0 = T \left({\mathbf 0}\right)$
(the last equality again by linearity), so injectivity gives $\sum_j c_j \mathbf e_j = \mathbf 0$,
whence $c_1 = \cdots = c_n = 0$ by Lemma 2.

By Lemma 3, therefore, $T \left({\mathbf e_1}\right), \ldots, T \left({\mathbf e_n}\right)$ spans
$\Bbb F^n$. Now let $\mathbf y \in \Bbb F^n$ be arbitrary and write
$\mathbf y = \sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n c_j T \left({\mathbf e_j}\right)$. By linearity,
$$\mathbf y = T \left({\sum_{j \mathop = 1}^n c_j \mathbf e_j}\right) ,$$
so $\mathbf y$ lies in the image of $T$. Hence $T$ is surjective. $\Box$

## 3. Proof of the Theorem

### Part 1: a left inverse is a right inverse

Let $\mathbf A, \mathbf B \in \mathcal M \left({n}\right)$ with $\mathbf{BA} = \mathbf I_n$.

**Step 1: $T_{\mathbf B} \circ T_{\mathbf A} = \operatorname{id}_{\Bbb F^n}$.** By (M5),
$$T_{\mathbf B} \circ T_{\mathbf A} = T_{\mathbf{BA}} = T_{\mathbf I_n} = \operatorname{id}_{\Bbb F^n} .$$

**Step 2: $T_{\mathbf A}$ is injective.** If $T_{\mathbf A} \left({\mathbf x}\right) = T_{\mathbf A} \left({\mathbf y}\right)$
then, applying $T_{\mathbf B}$ and using Step 1,
$$\mathbf x = T_{\mathbf B} \left({T_{\mathbf A} \left({\mathbf x}\right)}\right)
= T_{\mathbf B} \left({T_{\mathbf A} \left({\mathbf y}\right)}\right) = \mathbf y .$$

**Step 3: $T_{\mathbf A}$ is surjective.** By (M5) the map $T_{\mathbf A}$ is linear, and by Step 2
it is injective; so Lemma 4 applies. *(This is the step at which finite-dimensionality is
essential: Lemma 4 is exactly where the argument would break down for an infinite-dimensional
space; see Section 5.)*

**Step 4: $T_{\mathbf A} \circ T_{\mathbf B} = \operatorname{id}_{\Bbb F^n}$.** Let
$\mathbf y \in \Bbb F^n$. By Step 3 there is $\mathbf x \in \Bbb F^n$ with
$T_{\mathbf A} \left({\mathbf x}\right) = \mathbf y$. Then, using Step 1,
$$T_{\mathbf A} \left({T_{\mathbf B} \left({\mathbf y}\right)}\right)
= T_{\mathbf A} \left({T_{\mathbf B} \left({T_{\mathbf A} \left({\mathbf x}\right)}\right)}\right)
= T_{\mathbf A} \left({\mathbf x}\right) = \mathbf y .$$

**Step 5: $\mathbf{AB} = \mathbf I_n$.** For each $j \in \left\{{1, \ldots, n}\right\}$, by (M5),
Step 4 and (M2),
$$\left({\mathbf{AB}}\right) \mathbf e_j = T_{\mathbf{AB}} \left({\mathbf e_j}\right)
= \left({T_{\mathbf A} \circ T_{\mathbf B}}\right) \left({\mathbf e_j}\right) = \mathbf e_j = \mathbf I_n \mathbf e_j .$$
By (M4), $\mathbf{AB} = \mathbf I_n$. That is, $\mathbf B$ is a right inverse of $\mathbf A$.
$\blacksquare$

### Part 2: a right inverse is a left inverse

Let $\mathbf A, \mathbf B \in \mathcal M \left({n}\right)$ and let $\mathbf B$ be a right inverse of
$\mathbf A$, i.e. $\mathbf{AB} = \mathbf I_n$. This equation says precisely that $\mathbf A$ is a
*left* inverse of $\mathbf B$. Both $\mathbf A$ and $\mathbf B$ lie in
$\mathcal M \left({n}\right)$, and Part 1 was proved for an arbitrary ordered pair of matrices in
$\mathcal M \left({n}\right)$; applying it to the pair $\left({\mathbf B, \mathbf A}\right)$ in
place of $\left({\mathbf A, \mathbf B}\right)$ yields that $\mathbf A$ is a *right* inverse of
$\mathbf B$, i.e. $\mathbf{BA} = \mathbf I_n$. That is, $\mathbf B$ is a left inverse of
$\mathbf A$. $\blacksquare$

### Corollary

Let $\mathbf B$ be a left inverse **or** a right inverse of $\mathbf A$. Then by Parts 1 and 2,
$\mathbf{AB} = \mathbf{BA} = \mathbf I_n$, so $\mathbf B$ is a two-sided inverse of $\mathbf A$.
Moreover such $\mathbf B$ is unique, and indeed every one-sided inverse of $\mathbf A$ is the same
matrix: if $\mathbf{BA} = \mathbf I_n$ and $\mathbf{AC} = \mathbf I_n$, then by (M2) and (M1)
$$\mathbf B = \mathbf B \mathbf I_n = \mathbf B \left({\mathbf{AC}}\right)
= \left({\mathbf{BA}}\right) \mathbf C = \mathbf I_n \mathbf C = \mathbf C . \qquad \blacksquare$$

## 4. An independent proof of Part 1, via determinants

This proof uses three standard facts about the determinant
$\det : \mathcal M \left({n}\right) \to \Bbb F$ over a commutative ring (in particular a field):

* $\det \left({\mathbf{MN}}\right) = \det \left({\mathbf M}\right) \det \left({\mathbf N}\right)$;
* $\det \left({\mathbf I_n}\right) = 1$;
* the adjugate identity
 $\mathbf A \operatorname{adj} \left({\mathbf A}\right) = \operatorname{adj} \left({\mathbf A}\right) \mathbf A = \det \left({\mathbf A}\right) \mathbf I_n$,
 where $\operatorname{adj} \left({\mathbf A}\right)$ is the transpose of the matrix of cofactors
 (this identity is the Laplace expansion of $\det \mathbf A$ along a row or column, together with
 the vanishing of "alien cofactor" expansions).

Assume $\mathbf{BA} = \mathbf I_n$. Taking determinants,
$\det \left({\mathbf B}\right) \det \left({\mathbf A}\right) = \det \left({\mathbf I_n}\right) = 1$,
so $\det \left({\mathbf A}\right) \ne 0$ and, $\Bbb F$ being a field,
$\det \left({\mathbf A}\right)$ is invertible in $\Bbb F$. Set
$$\mathbf C := \det \left({\mathbf A}\right)^{-1} \operatorname{adj} \left({\mathbf A}\right) \in \mathcal M \left({n}\right) .$$
The adjugate identity, together with the compatibility of scalar and matrix multiplication, gives
$\mathbf{AC} = \mathbf{CA} = \mathbf I_n$. Therefore, by (M2) and (M1),
$$\mathbf B = \mathbf B \mathbf I_n = \mathbf B \left({\mathbf{AC}}\right) = \left({\mathbf{BA}}\right) \mathbf C
= \mathbf I_n \mathbf C = \mathbf C ,$$
and hence $\mathbf{AB} = \mathbf{AC} = \mathbf I_n$. $\blacksquare$

(Part 2 follows from Part 1 by the same symmetry argument as before.)

## 5. Sharpness of the hypotheses

* **Squareness is essential.** For rectangular matrices the analogous statement is false. Take
 $$\mathbf A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \in \mathcal M \left({2, 1}\right) , \qquad
 \mathbf B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \in \mathcal M \left({1, 2}\right) .$$
 Then $\mathbf{BA} = \left({1}\right) = \mathbf I_1$, while
 $\mathbf{AB} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \ne \mathbf I_2$.
* **Finite dimension is essential.** For linear operators on an infinite-dimensional space the
 statement fails. On the space $V$ of all sequences in $\Bbb F$, define the linear maps
 $R \left({x_1, x_2, \ldots}\right) = \left({0, x_1, x_2, \ldots}\right)$ and
 $L \left({x_1, x_2, \ldots}\right) = \left({x_2, x_3, \ldots}\right)$. Then
 $L \circ R = \operatorname{id}_V$, but $R \circ L \ne \operatorname{id}_V$, since
 $R \left({L \left({1, 0, 0, \ldots}\right)}\right) = \mathbf 0$. Correspondingly, $R$ is injective
 but not surjective: this is exactly the failure of Lemma 4, whose proof used the finiteness of the
 spanning list $\mathbf e_1, \ldots, \mathbf e_n$ (through Lemma 1).
* **Generality of the scalars.** The determinant proof of Section 4 uses only that the scalars form
 a commutative ring with unity, so the theorem holds verbatim in that generality (there
 $\det \left({\mathbf B}\right) \det \left({\mathbf A}\right) = 1$ shows $\det \left({\mathbf A}\right)$
 is a *unit*, which is what the argument needs). The proof of Section 3 also adapts to scalars
 forming a division ring, provided $\Bbb F^n$ is regarded as a *right* vector space (so that
 $\mathbf M \left({\mathbf x \lambda}\right) = \left({\mathbf M \mathbf x}\right) \lambda$) and the
 lemmas of Section 2 are stated for right vector spaces; the arguments given go through unchanged
 apart from placing scalars on the right. By contrast, over a general non-commutative ring the
 statement can fail, as the shift example above shows once it is realised as a pair of $1 \times 1$
 matrices over the endomorphism ring of an infinite-dimensional vector space.
